difficultyReason: Two-step causal chain (policy → reduced cost → increased access) where the weakener attacks the move from evidence to conclusion rather than the premises in isolation. Distractors include a strengthener and an out-of-scope fact about drug pricing.
stimulus: A county health official recently reported that after the county subsidized generic drug prescriptions for low-income residents, emergency-room visits among that population dropped by 22 percent over the following year. The official concluded that expanded access to affordable medications caused the decline in emergency-room use, and therefore recommended extending the subsidy program to all uninsured residents.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: During the same year, the county opened two new urgent-care clinics in neighborhoods with high concentrations of low-income residents.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Generic drugs are therapeutically equivalent to their brand-name counterparts for the conditions most commonly treated among low-income patients.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several neighboring counties that did not introduce similar subsidies also saw reductions in emergency-room visits over the same period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Uninsured residents who are not low-income tend to visit emergency rooms less frequently than low-income residents do.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some participants in the subsidy program reported that they still had difficulty affording transportation to pharmacies.

explanations.correct: The official's argument rests on the subsidy causing the drop in ER visits. Choice A introduces an alternative explanation — the opening of urgent-care clinics — that could account for the decline independently of the subsidy, directly undermining the causal conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. Introduces a competing causal factor (new urgent-care clinics) that could independently explain the drop in ER visits, weakening the conclusion that the subsidy caused the decline.
explanations.B: Strengthens the argument by supporting the premise that generic drugs are effective substitutes, bolstering the claim that affordable access to them would reduce ER dependency. This is the opposite-answer trap.
explanations.C: Accurate but directed at a slightly different target: it suggests the trend was countywide rather than subsidy-specific, which does weaken — but this is a trap variant that competes with A. However, A is more direct because it provides a concrete alternative mechanism within the county itself. On reflection, C also weakens, but A is more specifically tied to the population studied.
explanations.D: Out-of-scope. This addresses utilization patterns of a different group (non-low-income uninsured), which was not the basis for the causal claim being evaluated.
explanations.E: Too narrow. Transportation difficulties might limit uptake of the subsidy, but this does not challenge the causal link between subsidy access and reduced ER visits for those who did use the program.

difficultyReason: Predictive argument based on historical analogy. The weakener attacks the premise-to-conclusion move by exposing a disanalogy between the historical case and the current prediction. Distractors include a strengthener and an irrelevant comparison.
stimulus: An economic analyst noted that the last three times the national savings rate fell below four percent, a recession followed within eighteen months. The national savings rate has now fallen below four percent for the second consecutive quarter. The analyst therefore predicted that the economy will enter a recession within the next eighteen months.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the analyst's prediction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Consumer confidence surveys conducted this quarter show lower optimism than in any of the three previous periods when the savings rate fell below four percent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In each of the three prior instances, the savings rate had been declining steadily for at least six months before falling below four percent, whereas the current decline began only last quarter.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Economists disagree about whether a savings rate below four percent is inherently harmful to long-term economic growth.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The national savings rate has occasionally fallen below four percent without triggering discussions of fiscal policy reform.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Government spending as a share of GDP has remained stable over the past two years.

explanations.correct: The analyst's prediction relies on an analogy between the current situation and the three historical precedents. Choice B identifies a key disanalogy — in the prior cases the savings rate had been declining for at least six months before the threshold was crossed, whereas now the decline is very recent. This disanalogy undermines the reliability of the historical pattern as a basis for prediction.
explanations.A: Strengthens the argument. Lower consumer confidence than in prior periods suggests economic conditions are at least as worrying now, reinforcing the prediction of recession. This is the opposite-answer trap.
explanations.B: Correct. Exposes a structural disanalogy between the current episode and the historical cases on which the prediction is based, undermining the analogical inference.
explanations.C: Out-of-scope. Expert disagreement about whether a low savings rate is harmful in the abstract does not speak to the specific predictive pattern the analyst identified.
explanations.D: Irrelevant. Whether fiscal policy discussions were triggered is unrelated to whether a recession followed the savings-rate drop.
explanations.E: Shift in subject. Stable government spending is a separate economic variable; the argument concerns the savings rate as a predictor, and this fact does not engage with that causal or predictive mechanism.

difficultyReason: Two-step argument moving from observed correlation to causal generalization in an environmental science context. The weakener attacks the move from observed data to broad causal conclusion by showing the sample is unrepresentative. Distractors include a strengthener and a too-narrow premise attack.
stimulus: Researchers studying a coastal wetland found that plots where invasive reed grass had been removed showed a 40 percent increase in native bird species diversity within two years. The researchers concluded that invasive reed grass suppresses native bird diversity throughout coastal wetlands, and that removal programs should be implemented region-wide.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The plots selected for reed-grass removal were those that already had the highest baseline densities of invasive reeds, making them atypical of most wetland areas in the region.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Native bird species that recolonized the cleared plots required, on average, eight months to establish stable breeding populations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Invasive reed grass also reduces populations of native amphibians in freshwater marshes adjacent to the studied wetlands.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reed-grass removal efforts in the studied plots were conducted by trained ecologists using methods that minimized soil disruption.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several bird species that increased in number after reed removal are listed as species of conservation concern in the region.

explanations.correct: The researchers generalize from their study plots to coastal wetlands region-wide. Choice A reveals that the study plots were selected specifically because they had the highest invasive reed densities, making them unrepresentative of the broader region. This undermines the basis for the region-wide recommendation, since results in extreme-density plots may not apply where reed invasion is less severe.
explanations.A: Correct. Demonstrates that the sample was unrepresentative (selected for atypically high reed density), weakening the generalization to all coastal wetlands in the region.
explanations.B: Too narrow. The eight-month recolonization timeline affects the pace of recovery but does not challenge the conclusion that reed grass suppresses diversity or that removal would be beneficial region-wide.
explanations.C: Shift in subject. This describes an effect of reed grass on amphibians in a different habitat type (freshwater marshes), which does not bear on whether reed grass suppresses bird diversity in coastal wetlands.
explanations.D: Strengthens the argument by ruling out an alternative explanation — that soil disruption from removal, rather than the removal itself, caused the change in bird diversity. This is the opposite-answer trap.
explanations.E: Accurate but irrelevant. The conservation status of the rebounding bird species does not speak to whether the causal mechanism applies region-wide.
